title: Destructuring
summary: Destructuring pulls values out of arrays or objects into named variables.

subtopics.title: Object values
subtopics.explanation: Object destructuring reads properties by name, such as `const { name } = user`. The property name tells JavaScript which value to read. It is like taking a labeled item from a drawer. Use it when a function needs a few fields, but keep the original object when many values would make the declaration hard to scan. In a real page, read a display name with `const { name } = person` when that property is required.

subtopics.title: Array values
subtopics.explanation: Array destructuring reads values by position, such as `const [first, second] = colors`. The first variable gets the first item. It is like taking the first two things from a numbered queue. Use it when positions have clear meaning, such as a pair returned by a hook; otherwise named object properties are often clearer. In a real page, use `[first, second]` to capture two returned values whose positions have fixed meaning.

subtopics.title: Defaults
subtopics.explanation: A default value is used when the property is missing or has the value `undefined`. For example, `const { theme = "light" } = settings`. It is like having a spare choice when a labeled drawer is empty. A default does not replace `null`, so handle that separately if null is a possible value. In a real page, give a default only when the missing value has a useful standard choice.

subtopics.title: Rename a value
subtopics.explanation: Renaming lets the local variable use a clearer name: `const { id: userId } = user`. It does not rename the original property. It is like putting a new label on the item you carried to your desk. Choose a name that makes its role clear where it is used. In a real page, rename `{ id: userId }` when another `id` already exists in the current scope.

subtopics.title: Nested data
subtopics.explanation: Destructuring a nested object gives you a reference to its nested value; it does not recursively clone it. This is like unpacking a folder while keeping the papers inside shared. If code mutates a nested object, other parts of the app may observe the change. Prefer immutable updates when state is shared. In a real page, changing a nested object after destructuring can still change the shared original object.

foundations.overview: Destructuring is JavaScript syntax for unpacking values from arrays or objects into named variables. It can make code shorter when the names and positions are clear. Think of it like unpacking labeled items from a bag. Destructuring does not create a deep copy of nested objects, so changing a nested value may still affect the original data.
foundations.whyItMatters: Destructuring makes data access compact, but clarity matters more than shorter syntax. Defaults, names, and shared references affect what the code does.
foundations.browserPerspective: Destructuring is syntactic sugar the engine compiles down to ordinary property and index reads. There's no runtime magic — { a } = obj is just const a = obj.a under the hood, with defaults compiling to undefined checks.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Pulling fields from props, reading useState/useReducer tuples, importing named exports, accepting options objects in utility functions, and unpacking API responses into local variables.
foundations.businessImpact: Concise, readable unpacking reduces boilerplate and the bugs that come with repetitive property access, helping teams ship features faster with fewer typos.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Parameter destructuring makes function contracts explicit (you see exactly which fields are used) and defaults make APIs forgiving of missing data.
foundations.performanceImpact: Negligible — it compiles to the same property accesses you'd write by hand. Very deep nested patterns add a few extra reads but nothing meaningful.
commonUseCases: Unpacking React props and hook return tuples
Accepting and defaulting an options object in functions
Reading named fields from API response objects
Swapping variables and separating 'first vs rest'
Extract a few values from a settings record.
Read a pair returned from a state hook.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Default values apply for null as well as undefined.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Defaults only trigger when the value is exactly undefined. A null value is considered present, so the default is NOT used.
Objects are unpacked by key name, so order is irrelevant. Only ARRAY destructuring is positional.
If an intermediate object is undefined (e.g. user.address is missing), reaching into it throws a TypeError. Default the intermediate or guard first.

visualExplorer.title: Unpacking an object with renaming and defaults
visualExplorer.caption: Step through how const { name: userName, role = 'guest' } = user binds variables.

config.intro: Follow const { name: userName, role = 'guest' } = { name: 'Ada' } as the engine resolves each binding.

steps.name: Read the source object
steps.detail: The right side is { name: 'Ada' } — it has a name key but no role key.

steps.name: Match the 'name' key
steps.detail: The pattern says name: userName, so the value 'Ada' is bound to a NEW variable called userName.

steps.name: Look up the 'role' key
steps.detail: There is no role property, so the looked-up value is undefined.

steps.name: Apply the default
steps.detail: Because role is undefined, the default 'guest' is used, binding role = 'guest'.

steps.name: Result
steps.detail: Two variables exist: userName = 'Ada' and role = 'guest'. No variable named 'name' is created.

codeLab.title: Refactor verbose access into destructuring
codeLab.instructions: Rewrite formatUser so it destructures the user object in the parameter list: pull name, rename role to title with a default of 'member', and reach into address.city. Keep the same returned string.
hints: Destructure inside the parentheses: function formatUser({ ... }).
Rename with role: title and default it with = 'member'.
Nest a pattern for address: { city } to reach the city.

keyTakeaways: Object destructuring reads properties by name, such as `const { name } = user`.
Array destructuring reads values by position, such as `const [first, second] = colors`.
A default value is used when the property is missing or has the value `undefined`.
Renaming lets the local variable use a clearer name: `const { id: userId } = user`.
Destructuring a nested object gives you a reference to its nested value; it does not recursively clone it.
